headline: High risk of shared-workspace prompt injection and data leakage; capability conflicts and cascading errors are also material.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: OpenHands can read/write files in a Docker runtime and use MCP; Windsurf shares state via local filesystem and exposes clipboard/files. That creates a plausible content-to-instruction bridge if one agent consumes the other’s workspace artifacts. The pathway is not proven by docs alone, so I avoid high, but it exists in default-ish setups.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same mounted workspace or local filesystem
IF either agent parses file contents or MCP payloads as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Separate the agents into distinct workspaces
Disable clipboard-based handoff between agents
Require provenance tags on any file passed between agents
Review MCP server allowlists before enabling them
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction/data separation

B_data_leakage.rationale: OpenHands touches files mounted into its runtime and handles model provider API keys; Windsurf touches workspace files and open files, with shared state via local filesystem. If sensitive files are present in the shared workspace, both agents can access them, and either may upload content to its backend. That is a default-configuration leakage path, though not enough for high without stronger evidence of uncontrolled exfiltration.
conditions: IF sensitive files are mounted into the shared workspace
IF either agent sends file contents to its inference backend or connected model proxy
mitigations: Keep secrets out of the shared workspace
Use separate OS users or containers per agent
Restrict both agents to least-privilege directories
Rotate any API keys exposed in mounted files
requires-engineering: enforce DLP or redaction before model upload

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell commands, write the filesystem, modify git state, install packages, and use broad network egress. OpenHands isolates per runtime, but Windsurf runs as the user with no self-isolation and shares state via local filesystem, so concurrent writes to the same repo can race and corrupt git or files. The overlap is broad enough that default use is dangerous.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or directory
IF either agent performs git commits, rebases, or package installs without coordination
mitigations: Run only one writer at a time
Use separate branches per agent
Lock the repo before edits
Disable auto-install in one agent
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level file and git locks

D_cascading_error.rationale: OpenHands can produce shell/browser-driven outputs, and Windsurf’s Cascade loop can act on workspace content with approval-per-command or auto-execute opt-in. If Windsurf treats OpenHands output as authoritative, errors can cascade into edits, installs, or commits. Because both agents are action-capable and the verification step is not guaranteed, the blast radius is substantial.
conditions: IF Windsurf consumes OpenHands-generated files or summaries as ground truth
IF auto-execute is enabled or command approvals are routinely accepted without review
mitigations: Require human review before acting on the other agent’s output
Pass only structured, validated artifacts between agents
Disable auto-execute in Windsurf
Keep OpenHands outputs in read-only review folders
requires-engineering: add verification gates before downstream actions

E_compliance.rationale: OpenHands is open-source and runs in a Docker runtime by default, while Windsurf is closed-source and runs in the editor process with broad workspace access. The pair can therefore place the same files under different retention, logging, and residency regimes, especially if model-provider or proxy services differ. The compliance mismatch is plausible but not specific enough for high.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in the shared workspace
IF the two agents route prompts or file contents through different vendors or regions
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the pair’s workspace
Document each vendor’s retention and residency settings
Use the same approved model region for both agents
Review logging settings before enabling the pair
requires-engineering: perform a formal data-flow and DPA review
